segments.say: Anton is back in his armchair with his tea, and the book is closed on his knee. He's not doing anything in particular. And, as it turns out, neither is his brain, at least in the way that scientists once understood it.

For a long time, the common assumption was simple. When you do a task, parts of the brain switch on. When you stop, they switch off. Rest was thought of as a blank baseline, a sort of idling engine, and the interesting science was whatever happened when the engine was asked to do something.

But in the 1990s, researchers using brain imaging began to notice something odd. When people were asked to do a focused task, such as looking at words or solving a puzzle, some regions of the brain did switch on. But a different set of regions switched off, or at least became less active, compared with when people were simply lying quietly in the scanner.

What made it striking was that the same regions kept showing up, in study after study, regardless of the task. A group of areas along the middle of the brain, towards the front and the back, always seemed more active when nothing was being asked of the person, and quieter when attention was needed elsewhere. The pattern was so consistent that it couldn't be an accident.

show.sub: The same regions, again and again

segments.say: In 2001, the neurologist Marcus Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis published a paper that gave this pattern a name. They called it a default mode of brain function. Their idea was that when you're not engaged in an outside task, the brain doesn't go quiet. It falls back to a default way of operating, which is active and organized, and which seems to matter.

show.what: Brain imaging showed a consistent set of regions that were more active at rest than during focused tasks

segments.say: One striking point that came out of that line of research concerns energy. Raichle and others noted that the brain uses a great deal of energy even at rest, and that the extra energy used when we take on a demanding task is quite small by comparison, usually just a few percent. The brain isn't switching on when you give it something to do. It's already running, all the time.

The set of regions came to be called the default mode network. It includes parts of the medial prefrontal cortex, towards the front of the brain, and the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, towards the back, along with regions in the parietal lobes and the inner temporal lobes, including the hippocampus. It's a team, and it works together.

And then came the obvious question. If the brain spends so much effort on this network when we're apparently doing nothing, what is it doing? One of the first suggestions was that it might be the home of mind wandering itself. When we're not focused on the outside world, we turn our attention inward, and this network seems to be where we do that.

In 2007, the psychologist Malia Mason and her colleagues ran an experiment that made the link directly. Volunteers practiced a simple task until it was automatic, and then did it, or a new version of it, in the scanner. When the task was easy and well practiced, people reported more wandering thoughts, and the default network was more active. The title of their paper said it plainly: wandering minds and the default network.

show.what: People practiced a task until it became automatic, then did it in the scanner while their reports of wandering thoughts were recorded

segments.say: The clever part of the design was that the difficulty of the task was changed, while everything else stayed similar. An easy, practiced task left spare mental room, and the mind used it to wander. A new, unfamiliar one demanded full attention, and the wandering faded. And the brain activity followed.

show.sub: A task that lets you drift

segments.say: That's one way of putting what they found. When the outside world asks for less, the mind turns inward, and the default network lights up.

show.text: When the world asks for less, the inner world begins to speak.
show.by: a way of putting the finding

segments.say: But the story got more complicated, in an interesting way. In 2009, Kalina Christoff and her colleagues at the University of British Columbia published a study in PNAS that used experience sampling during brain scanning. They interrupted people mid-task, at random, and asked whether their minds had been wandering. Then they looked at the brain activity just before each interruption.

show.sub: It isn't only the default network

segments.say: They found that the default network was indeed more active before people reported wandering. But they also found something more surprising. A set of regions linked with executive control, the parts that help us plan and hold goals in mind, were active too. And they were most active when people hadn't noticed that their minds had wandered.

show.what: Experience sampling during fMRI compared brain activity before reported mind wandering with brain activity during focused reading

segments.say: That finding changed the picture. It suggested that mind wandering isn't simply the brain going slack. In some cases, the control regions of the brain are quietly working alongside the default network, which suggests that a wandering mind may be busy rather than lazy. It's a different kind of busyness, directed inwards, and not always supervised.

Seen from a hill at night, a city never really turns off. Windows glow in a thousand small squares, and traffic moves like slow threads of light. From the outside, it looks quiet. Up close, it's full of activity, only none of it is aimed at you.

show.cap: A city at night, lights still on

segments.say: Many scientists use a similar image for the resting brain. From a distance it looks calm, but it's full of hidden activity, much of it quietly organizing memories, rehearsing futures and keeping a running sense of who you are. It's a city at night. Not asleep, only turned inward.

show.sub: A city that never switches off

segments.say: In 2008, the neuroscientists Randy Buckner, Jessica Andrews-Hanna and Daniel Schacter wrote a major review of the network for the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. They described how the same regions seem to be involved in remembering the past, imagining the future, thinking about other people's minds, and wandering through the many possible things we could be doing. In other words, it's the network of the inner life.

In the armchair, Anton lets his eyes rest on the lamp. If the research is right, his default network is quite busy right now, quietly turning over the afternoon, the week ahead, and the small things he's forgotten to do. He isn't wasting time. He's doing what a brain does when it has nothing else to do, which is to keep thinking.

But what happens to the outside world while the mind is away? Next, we'll look at what researchers have found when people zone out in the middle of reading, and why they can look at a page and see nothing.
